newsitem.title: GERMANY: Germany's Waigel optimistic on tax reform talks.
newsitem.headline: Germany's Waigel optimistic on tax reform talks.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said on Sunday he was optimistic that agreement could be reached on a planned major reform of Germany's tax system at talks with opposition politicians later this month.
Waigel was quoted in the Welt am Sonntag newspaper as saying he was confident of "an agreement by the middle of this year on the first part of the reform for January 1, 1998."

Waigel's comments come as the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), who will be present at the talks, laid down concrete conditions for agreeing the package, aimed at cutting taxes by a net total of 30 billion marks ($17.8 billion).

"No taxes on nightshift and holiday bonuses...and no reduction in the top rate of tax from 53 percent to 39 percent for private incomes. These are our conditions," Peter Struck, parliamentary business manager of the SPD, was quoted by Welt am Sonntag as saying.

New taxes on currently tax-free unsociable working hours were intended as one way of financing wide reductions in taxes elsewhere in the package, which includes a cut in the entry rate of income tax and lower corporate taxes.

The talks, planned for February 24, were announced on Thursday as a means of breaking the political deadlock over the reform, which Bonn is counting on to boost investment in the economy and help fight Germany's growing unemployment problem.

The talks, at which Chancellor Helmut Kohl will meet SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine, have however been treated warily by Kohl's junior coalition partners, the Free Democrats (FDP), who do not want any watering down of the reform.
FDP parliamentary leader Hermann Solms said the talks would show whether Lafontaine would seek to hinder the reform with "unacceptable conditions".
Solms further urged the government to implement the whole of the tax reform in 1998, earlier than the 1999 by which the bulk of the package is due to be in force.
In an newspaper interview published on Saturday, Kohl said he was "absolutely convinced" that the tax reform, together with unpopular planned changes to the German pension system, would go ahead.
